lesson_title: The Month-End Test: Liquidity, Solvency and the Owner's Return
hook_text: You can't pay the landlord in rice. That's a real accounting ratio.
clip_script: Every family knows the month-end test. Bills lining up at the door — rent, electricity, the account at the shop. On the table: incoming money, the food in the cupboard, what your cousin owes you. Can what's coming in cover what's knocking? Business calls that the current ratio. But a careful mother sharpens it: 'the cupboard counts, but I can't pay the landlord in rice.' Strip out the stock — it still needs a buyer — and ask again with only the near-cash things. THAT'S the acid test. Then the bigger, quieter question for hard times: if we had to settle everything by selling everything, would there be enough? Solvency. And finally the owner's own question: my money lived in this shop all year and earned thirty-six percent — the bank pays eight. Worth it? Almost — but the bank's eight is promised, and the shop's thirty-six was sweated for. Risk deserves its wage. Three household questions. Three famous ratios. Same test.
visual_style: A kitchen table at month-end: bills stacking at the door, resources laid out and sorted; rice bag greying out for the acid test; the house weighed on scales for solvency; two jars — bank 8% vs shop 36% — for the finale.
mood: Grounded, familial, quietly empowering — accounting as street wisdom.
pacing: Three-act structure, one question per act, tightening to the risk-deserves-wages punchline.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run all three tests on a real business.
